title: CXCon 2026: Customer Experience Is Built Long Before the Complaint
summary: At CXCon 2026, Lagos Business School, Chowdeck, Kuda and Cowrywise leaders explained why great customer experience is engineered long before a complaint
body_markdown:
When an automated savings debit fails on Cowrywise, the customer gets an email. For a long time, it said: “your payment failed.” Recently, it started saying “your payment didn’t go through.”


At CXCon 2026, an attendee stood up to say she had noticed. She saves automatically, and when her bank account is empty, the debit fails. The old wording made her feel as though the failure was hers. The new wording didn’t. “It’s no longer my failure,” she said.


The change was small, but its effect was noticeable. Even the wording of an automated email can shape how a customer experiences an already stressful moment. It was a fitting illustration of the argument that would run through CXCon 2026: great customer experiences are built through deliberate decisions, often long before something goes wrong.


Held on October 16, 2026, at Landmark Centre in Lagos, the third edition of CXCon drew close to 1,000 attendees, under the theme “Engineering Experiences.” Across a keynote, two panels and a founders’ fireside, three ideas kept returning:


1. Customer experience is created across the entire organisation, not just in customer support.
2. Businesses should eliminate recurring friction instead of resolving the same complaints again and again.
3. How a company responds when something fails is the real test of the experience it has built.


“Great experiences don’t happen by accident. They are intentionally engineered,” said Enor Izomor, Associate Vice President, Customer Experience at Cowrywise and the conference’s convener.


## **Why this matters now**


Professor Uchenna Uzo of Lagos Business School opened the conference by challenging businesses to rethink customer loyalty. “People are not as loyal as they used to be,” he said, arguing that competitive pricing alone is no longer enough to retain customers who have more alternatives and rising expectations.


When Uzo asked the room whether price or experience did more to keep customers loyal, most hands went up for price. The research pointed the other way. Price matters, he said, but only to a point. Customers are increasingly willing to choose a more expensive option that offers a better experience, even if it means buying less often, and their expectations keep rising.


If customers increasingly choose businesses based on their experiences, the next question is who in a business is actually responsible for creating them. The answer from the stage was consistent: Everyone.


## **1. Customer experience is created across the organisation**


“A customer doesn’t separate your product from your payment process, your communication, your policies or how you handle a problem,” Enor said. “They experience all of it as one relationship with your business.”


Edememe Oladiji-Wusu, CEO of Semper Discens, made the same point during the panel on how CX wins in tough markets. A customer visiting your premises will remember how the gateman treated them and whether there was space to park, not only how the support agent sounded. “Gone are the days when CX was the responsibility of just the CX people,” she said.


At the founders’ fireside, Femi Aluko, Co-founder and CEO of Chowdeck, described how his company builds that into its operations. Every new hire, however senior, makes deliveries and answers customer support tickets in their first week, and the whole company does it again every quarter.


“It’s very easy to lose empathy as an engineer, as a designer, as a marketer if you don’t face these things as regularly as the customer experience team does,” he said.


At Gazmadu, Founder and CEO Yagazie Eguare puts new team members through a client session themselves and shares client impact stories with everyone, down to the cleaner.


If experience belongs to the whole organisation, so does the knowledge customer-facing teams collect. Oluwatobi Ojo, Managing Director of Notch HR, described pulling her support team into product and engineering sessions that usually include only developers and QA. “They have the answers to what those guys are looking for,” she said.


Razaq Ahmed, Co-founder and CEO of Cowrywise, argued that this is exactly why businesses should rethink who they put in those roles. He pointed out that a CX vacancy can attract tens of thousands of applicants, while an iOS engineering role attracts a handful. In his view, the gap reflects a mistaken belief that anyone can do customer experience, and that it is a role people fall into when they have no other options rather than a profession in its own right.


“If there is a team that should be occupied by the most intelligent people in the organisation, it should be the team that the customers interact with,” he said.


## **2. Fix the friction, not just the complaint**


Owning the experience across a business is one thing. Acting on what customers keep telling you is another, and it is where many businesses get stuck.


Linda Apesin, Head of Customer Experience and Operations at Credit Direct, argued that the goal of customer experience is a journey so smooth that customers rarely need support. By the time a customer raises a complaint, something in the experience has already fallen short, and the support team is often recovering that experience rather than creating it.


She described one fix from earlier in her career. Financial institutions were flooding a contact centre with emails. Hiring more agents would have kept pace with the volume without reducing it. Instead, the team built a self-service portal that answered simple enquiries automatically and checked transaction status through APIs. Volume fell, and partners trusted the company more because they could see what was happening without having to ask.


The solution wasn’t to answer more enquiries. It was to eliminate the need for many of those enquiries in the first place.


Chowdeck learned the same lesson the expensive way. When it began delivering from traditional bukkas, tickets kept arriving about missing beef, and for two weeks the company kept issuing refunds. The beef was there. The pieces were so small that customers mistook them for beans or part of the sauce. The real fix was a photo and a clearer menu description, not another refund.


The career panel turned this into a habit any CX professional can build. Chinedu Udeze, User Experience Research Manager at Moniepoint, said growth starts with curiosity, and with one question in particular: “Why did this customer support ticket land on my desk in the first place?” Norah Ikoh, Head of Customer Experience Operations at Kuda Microfinance Bank, pushed it further. If the same issue has arrived for six months, she said, stop asking how to resolve it again and start asking how to stop it recurring.


Cowrywise’s own CX team has been working through the same shift. Oluboye Adekunle, a senior customer experience specialist who moderated the tough-markets panel, said customers repeatedly told the team that delays and follow-ups made already stressful situations worse. Rather than simply replying faster, the team redesigned the processes behind those requests. The team has since automated more than five CX processes, helping it track requests more clearly, reduce repetitive tasks and respond more consistently.


It is ongoing work, not a finished one. “Great CX isn’t just about being friendly when a customer reaches out; it is about designing the journey so fewer customers have to struggle in the first place,” Oluboye said.


## **3. The real test comes when something fails**


Fixing recurring problems can prevent many complaints. But even the most thoughtfully designed systems will sometimes fail. What happens next is another part of the experience businesses must engineer.


Uzo opened his keynote with two stories. In the first, he took a boat to Tarkwa Bay. Halfway there, the engine died. When he asked the operator what he planned to do, the answer was an offer to refund the fare. “If you return my money to me, what am I going to do with it?” Uzo recalled.


In the second, Amazon delivered a large order of books to Pan-Atlantic University late, ahead of an accreditation visit. The company delivered anyway, sent a letter of apology and refunded the full amount.


The real measure of how well a company engineers experiences, Uzo said, is what it does “when something bad happens.” When he asked how many people in the room had ever received an apology and a full refund from a service provider, two hands went up.


The panellists described what good recovery looks like. Customers, Apesin said, “don’t want to hear the sorries. They want to hear what happened, what you’re doing about it, and how soon it will be done.”


Toun Akinsunmi, Director of Customer Success and Chief of Staff at Seamless Technologies, gave the room a framework for the trust that survives a failure: **PACT** , which stands for predictability, accountability, consistency and transparency. A basic app that behaves the same way every time, she argued, earns more loyalty than a beautiful one that doesn’t.


That kind of reliability has to be designed in advance. Asked what leaders should examine every Monday morning, Apesin told them to walk the unhappy path: what happens when a button fails, what message the customer sees and what they are expected to do next. Akinsunmi warned against relying on dashboards alone. Metrics such as NPS are lagging indicators, and by the time churn shows up in the numbers, the damage has been done.


## **From the stage to practice**


Beyond the discussions onstage, CXCon offered examples of how deliberate experience design can shape the event itself and create opportunities beyond it.


CoinQuest, a networking game developed by Cowrywise’s engineering team, turned a familiar conference activity into an interactive experience. Attendees earned rewards for meeting other participants, with 708 people making 16,013 connections in approximately six hours, according to[the team that built it](https://engineering.cowrywise.com/article/coinquest-cx-con-26) .


The event’s impact has also extended beyond the conference itself. Sixteen days after attending CXCon 2025, Sarah joined Cowrywise as a customer experience specialist. A year later, she is a senior specialist. The 2026 edition ended with another invitation for interested professionals to explore opportunities with the company.


CXCon itself has followed the same path from talking to doing. It began in 2024 as a conversation about CX excellence and business growth. This year, it focused on how customer experiences are designed, delivered and improved.


“We don’t need more businesses simply saying they are customer-centric,” Enor said. “We need more businesses building the systems, cultures and capabilities to prove it.”


That proof isn’t found in support metrics alone. It shows up in the email that no longer makes a customer feel blamed, the complaint that stops arriving, and the moment something breaks and the customer stays anyway.
